Mapping current species richness. We estimated the range of taxa based on georeferenced occurrences, excluding those retrieved from administrative entities. First, we drew alpha-hull shapes around occurrences with an alpha radius = 1000 km, allowing us to retrieve disjunct ranges in case occurrences formed distant clusters. Next, we applied a taxon-specific buffer around alpha-hulls based on the density of sampling for each taxon using a minimal buffer of one arc-degree, and a maximum buffer estimated as the 80% quantile of minimal pairwise distances between occurrences as a way to account for uncertainty in the sampling of the actual species range89. Finally, we rasterized and stacked all buffered alpha-hulls representing taxon ranges and computed local species richness as the sum of taxon presence recorded in each quarter-degree cell to obtain a map of worldwide ponerine species richness.

Historical biogeography
Bioregional scheme. Each occurrence was attributed to a bioregion based on the bioregion scheme used in AntWeb (https://www.antweb.org/). We lumped Madagascar with the Afrotropics and split the Palearctic between Western and Eastern Palearctic to ensure a more homogeneous split of terrestrial areas. The latter also allowed discrimination of Nearctic/Palearctic dispersal through the Bering land bridge in the Northern Pacific or the Thule land bridge in the Northern Atlantic. We also classified India and the Burmese terrane under a unique Indo Malayan bioregion, even though those territories have been allegedly separated over geological time90. The vast majority of ponerines found in the present-day Burmese area and in the Indian subcontinent are also encroaching on the surrounding South-Asian regions, limiting vastly the informative power of historical biogeographic inferences treating those areas as separate entities. This treatment also ensures a more balanced area division of terrestrial lands. Recent investigations of current native ant bioregionalization have identified sets of different bioregions91,92 that remain largely concomitant with the broad delineation we used. Such delineations are based on the current distribution of taxa but are less suitable for use in historical biogeographic analyses accounting for continental drift and investing taxon distributions over evolutionary time. Thus, we favored the use of our larger bioregion scheme in line with past and recent endeavors in zooregionalization and historical biogeography31,93–97. Binary tables of presence/absence of the 1534 ponerine ant taxa across bioregions used in this study are available in Supplementary Data S6.

Ancestral range estimates with BioGeoBEARS. To study support for the Time-for-Accumulation Hypothesis (TfAH), we estimated the ancestral ranges of ponerine ants in our exhaustive phylogeny. We ran a set of time-stratified historical biogeographic models within the BioGeoBEARS framework accounting for different combinations of biogeographic events such as range expansion and contraction, vicariance, subset speciation, and jump-dispersal, with DIVALIKE, DIVALIKE+J, DEC, and DEC+J models98. Such a time-stratified approach accounts for changes in bioregion connectivity by providing adjacency matrices (Supplementary Data S7) associated with each geological epoch and preventing lineages from harboring ranges encompassing non-adjacent bioregions at any given point in time. Although we acknowledge that +J models may yield unrealistically low regional extinction rates and tend to limit the residence times of widespread ranges99, they also allow long-distance jump-dispersal events concomitant with speciation (i.e., founder effect) to occur, even between non-adjacent areas. This releases an important, and likely unrealistic, constraint of other models with the j parameter set to 0 that prevents any dispersal to occur between non-adjacent areas. Therefore, we chose to rely on likelihood-based statistical comparison to select the best-fitting model for our analyses100 and ran a whole set of models as listed above, without a priori deciding which one should be favored.

The DEC+J model was selected as the best model across both the grafted MCC tree and all 1000 grafted time-calibrated phylogenies, accounting for uncertainty in both divergence dating and taxon grafting, including the youngest and oldest divergence dating hypotheses (Mean Akaike’s weight = 99.95%; Supplementary Tables S1–S4). Similarly, ancestral range estimates based on posterior marginal likelihoods using those fitted DEC+J models appeared congruent across all phylogenies (Supplementary Tables S5–S8). Therefore, we conducted all downstream analyses on the grafted MCC tree under the DEC+J model. In parallel, we performed sensitivity analyses by conducting the same analytical pipeline on both the youngest and oldest divergence dating hypotheses in order to fully assess the robustness of our conclusions to alternative divergence age estimates. We also employed the Cohen’s Kappa index for classification similarity (Cohen, 1960) to quantify agreement in the most likely ancestral range estimated for shared nodes between the different divergence dating hypotheses (i.e., MCC, Youngest, and Oldest).

Biogeographic stochastic mapping (BSM). We applied Biogeographic Stochastic Mapping101 (BSM) using the best-fitted model for historical biogeography (DEC+J) to simulate 1000 possible biogeographic histories for ponerine ants on the grafted MCC tree. BSM draws random ranges at each internal node based on the estimated posterior marginal probabilities, then simulates range evolution on each branch using estimated state transition parameters until it finds a biogeographic history compatible with allowed ranges. From BSM simulations, we retrieved the posterior frequencies of anagenetic and cladogenetic events and recorded the sources and destinations of dispersal events in time. In particular, we quantified the counts and relative frequencies of events along 10 My sliding windows to compare dispersal dynamics in time across bioregions and investigate support for the Asymmetrical Dispersal Hypothesis (ADH). In the case of ranges encompassing multiple bioregions, the lineages were equally divided among the bioregions to contribute to respective bioregional counts.

Mapping biogeographic and diversification dynamics through time. To visualize the overall dynamic of ponerine ants in space and time, we constructed paleomaps of bioregions based on a geological model of continental plate drift102 implemented in the rgplates R package103. We then overlaid the network of dispersal events across moving bioregions at each time step (1 My), with edge width scaled by event counts recorded within time-windows of 5 My, and vertex size scaled by regional species richness quantified as number of lineages present in each region at each time step, aggregated across the 1000 BSM simulations. The final animation of ponerine ant biogeographic and diversification dynamics is available in Supplementary Movie 1.

Diversification dynamics
Empirical in situ speciation rates. Complementary to frequencies of dispersal events, we also recorded the source of cladogenetic events and quantified the frequencies and rates of in situ speciation as the number of range inheritance events within time-sliding windows. As with dispersal events, ranges encompassing multiple bioregions contributed equally to respective bioregional counts.

BAMM diversification rates. Besides empirical speciation rates estimated from in situ speciation event counts on time-calibrated phylogenies, we also used BAMM v2.5.0 to estimate diversification rates among lineages using a mechanistic approach modeling rate shifts104. Several independent runs with four reversible-jump MCMC on 107 generations were carried out for 1, 5, 10, and 20 expected number of shifts, with all other priors set to default using the R package BAMMtools v2.1.1228. We combined the output of the four chains in each run and confirmed that all analyses converged by visually examining the posterior traces of parameters (Supplementary Fig. S16) and ensuring effective sample size (ESS) for each parameter was above 200. We sampled 1000 posterior generations after discarding burn-in and selected the run with 10 expected shifts for downstream analyses since its prior distribution was the most similar to the posterior. From this, we obtained 1000 evolutionary scenarios from which we retrieved median diversification rates along branches (Supplementary Figs. S14 and S15). We compared median rates estimated for the grafted MCC tree and the alternative divergence dating hypotheses using Spearman’s sum-rank correlation tests across branches associated with shared clades. Estimated rates were aggregated per bioregion membership, as estimated from the BSM simulations, to compute rates through time evolution in relation to bioregions31. For the MCC tree, we recovered on average 12.1 ± 4.1 regime shifts in diversification dynamics along ponerine ant history, of which seven concerned major radiations (see Supplementary Table S10 for regime shifts metadata from the Maximum Shift Credibility (MSC) configuration).

BAMM, and other similar methods used to estimate time-varying diversification rates and identify regime shifts suffer from identifiability issues105. To limit potential issues, we focused our analyses on net diversification rates rather than on the absolute estimation of speciation and extinction rates individually. As a Bayesian approach, BAMM samples a large number of alternative diversification histories that can lead to similar likelihood, effectively accounting for a portion of the uncertainty regarding the identification of the “real” diversification history. Such uncertainty was carried out down to our tests for diversification rate differences as we performed STRAPP tests across posterior BAMM samples (see Section 9.1 below). Additionally, we combined BAMM analyses with a different approach based on Regional In-Situ Radiations (see Section 9.2 below) in order to cross-validate our results and address identifiability issues to the best possible extent.

Mapping current diversification rates. To visualize the spatial distribution of current diversification rates, we assigned taxon-specific rates estimated from BAMM to each respective taxon range, as estimated from buffered alpha-hulls, and extracted the mean current rates recorded among taxa found in each quarter-degree grid cell. To limit artifactual outlier values, we recorded mean rates only for grid cells with more than two taxa. Additionally, we extracted mean rates along latitudinal and longitudinal bands of one arc-degree based on taxa with a range overlapping each band. We extracted such geographic gradients across all 1000 BAMM posterior samples and generated a null distribution of mean rates along gradients by permuting species identities among range data. We identified latitudinal and longitudinal bands where the mean current diversification rates are lower/higher than expected if species were distributed randomly.

Diversification-dispersal relationships
BAMM rates across bioregions: STRAPP tests. We carried out STRAPP tests using the traitDependentBAMM function in the R package BAMMtools v2.1.1228 to investigate differences in current diversification rates across bioregions and formally test for support for the Diversification Rate Hypothesis (DRH). For greater statistical power, we focused on differences between temperate and tropical bioregions along a latitudinal gradient and between the Old World and the New World along a longitudinal gradient (Fig. 5), but also report results considering the seven bioregions altogether (Supplementary Information Fig. S10). Such a test permutes tip rates across taxa in the posterior samples from a BAMM analysis using a block-design that accounts for the non-independence of tip rates data via permutations restricted among macroevolutionary regimes106. Then, statistics from two-sided Wilcoxon tests (for pairwise gradient tests) and Kruskal-Wallis tests (across all bioregions) are compared to the value obtained from the observed data to assess significance of rate differences against random rate distribution across regimes.

Additionally, we designed a modified version of the STRAPP test that allows us to test for diversification rate differences through evolutionary time, and not only between present-day rates, as those are unlikely to be informative about long-term past dynamics shaping biodiversity32,107. We used bioregion membership estimates from the BSM simulations and cut off the phylogenies mapped with biogeographic histories every 0.1 My time step to be able to carry out STRAPP tests across lineages present at any given point in time. As a result, we obtained p-values for rate differences along evolutionary time and could identify timeframes of significance.

RISR analyses. To identify the main factors explaining differences in diversification rates across bioregions, we investigated the diversification dynamics of Regional In Situ Radiations (RISR). RISR are independent clades that diversify almost exclusively within a unique bioregion, allowing for statistical tests between evolutionary independent units31. First, we identified RISR as clades whose lineages spent more than 75% of cumulated time along branches in a single bioregion, with a minimum of 10 extant taxa. As such, we identified 9 RISR in Afrotropics, 5 in Australasia, 12 in Indomalaya, and 5 in Neotropics. For each clade, we fitted a time-dependent birth-death model with speciation rates (λ) being an exponential function of time since the crown age (t=0) and extinction rates (μ) being constants similar to macroevolutionary regimes in BAMM104 (Eqs. 1, 2 and 3). Models were fitted with the R package diversitree v0.10-1108. (Eqs. 1, 2, 3 omitted).

We extracted the crown age, the crown net diversification rate (R_crown), the current net diversification rate (R_current), and the time-variation parameter (α) associated with each RISR. We then tested for differences in parameter values across bioregions using two-sided Kruskal–Wallis and pairwise post hoc Wilcoxon tests. Finally, we used a Poisson regression to predict present-day taxonomic richness of RISR across bioregions based on crown ages.

Quantifying lineage origins through time. We designed a new method to estimate and map the age of immigration for lineages within a new bioregion and gather additional support for the Time-for-Accumulation Hypothesis (TfAH). We browsed our 1000 BSM simulations from tips-to-root to retrieve for each present-day taxon, the timing of the range shift when the lineage reached its current bioregion for the first time. For taxa harboring a range encompassing multiple bioregions, the “biogeographic immigration age” is averaged between areas. Taxon immigration ages were then averaged across all simulations. As with current diversification rates, we mapped the spatial distribution of biogeographic immigration ages using taxon ranges as estimated from buffered alpha-hulls and extracted the mean immigration ages of taxa recorded in each quarter-degree grid cell. To limit artifactual outlier values, we recorded mean ages only for grid cells with more than two taxa. Additionally, we computed geographic gradients of mean ages along latitudinal and longitudinal bands of one arc-degree based on taxa with a range overlapping each band. For statistical comparison, we generated a null distribution of mean immigration ages along geographic gradients by permuting species identities among range data.

Finally, we investigated changes through time in the origin of lineages across bioregions. Using the BSM simulations, we recorded at each time step (1 My) the origin of lineages found in each bioregion. The origins were examined by comparing the lineage ranges at the focal time step with the range of their most direct parental node. Autochthonous scores of each lineage were computed as the proportion of unique areas in the lineage range found among the unique areas of its parental range. Then we computed the mean autochthonous score per bioregion by aggregating lineages across their focal time ranges, splitting lineages equally among bioregions in the case of ranges encompassing multiple areas. As such, for each time step and each bioregion, we obtained mean autochthonous scores representing the counts and proportions of lineages present at a given time step whose presence is due to in situ diversification as opposed to dispersal.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The authors present an impressive and comprehensive phylogeny of the ant subfamily Ponerinae—the largest ever assembled for this clade—and use this newly constructed tree to explore its biogeographic history, with a particular focus on dispersal events and diversification patterns. The dataset (in terms of loci) and manuscript (in terms of number of analyses) are of high quality. The authors emphasize why non-vertebrate taxa should be investigated to better understand global biodiversity patterns. However, while the study is engaging, we have several concerns that we believe preclude publication in Nature Communications, at least in its current form. We (the reviewers) are an early career researcher and a senior researcher with complementary skills and knowledge in insect biogeography and diversification analyses. We reviewed the manuscript separately, before exchanging our opinions, and had the same overall sense of the limitations of this work, limitations that primarily relate to the level of novelty and support of the main results. We have summarised our comments below, first with our main points and then with some more specific suggestions, mainly on additional analyses that should be carried out to fully support the hypotheses and conclusions of the manuscript, especially in light of methodological concerns raised in recent studies (e.g., Louca and Pennell, 2020 - Nature).

1) While we acknowledge the considerable amount of work and the production of the most comprehensive phylogenetic hypothesis for Ponerinae, we have concerns about the novelty of the main results of this study. Importantly, the discussion highlights the role of the Time-for-Accumulation Hypothesis (TfAH) in explaining the latitudinal diversity gradient of this ant subfamily. This has already been found in Economo et al. (2018 – Nat. Comm.) at the whole scale of ants. As Economo et al. (2018) is surprisingly not reported in the introduction, the novelty of this study in this respect was unclear to us. We could see that the methodological approaches were different and that here, for instance, biogeographic analyses were carried out, but it was not always clear what each set of analyses brings to the overall narrative and what is completely new and what supports previous knowledge/hypotheses.
2) Somewhat related to our first point, we were confused by what seemed to us to be a rather strong disconnection between the introduction and the discussion of this manuscript. Overall, we were not well prepared by the introduction to fully grasp what was really at stake—the abstract with a single sentence of context did not help. And the relatively short discussion did not emphasize the novelties enough, whereas some of the ‘key findings’ seem like very general statements or truisms (e.g. line 529, which states that “this study highlights the importance of reconstructing the timing of past biogeographic and evolutionary events”).
3) “Timing is everything”. This work emphasizes the importance of timing, but we feel that the uncertainties surrounding Dating analyses are not as advanced as they should be. A reliable and credibly dated phylogeny is essential for assessing diversification rate shifts and the biogeographic history of lineages. There are also increasing examples of how the inclusion of fossil taxa can alter datings, diversification and biogeographic analyses. The authors do report and briefly explain why they did not use fossils, but how and to what extent this may affect their main results and conclusions is only touched upon.
4) Bioregions. The authors used 7 bioregions in several maps and some analyses. But when it comes to testing latitudinal and longitudinal gradients, they only use 2 bioregions (temperate vs tropical and Old World vs New World, respectively). This choice is motivated by statistical reasons (line 264), but there is no critical discussion or sensitivity analyses to explain how harmless this important choice is (or is not).
5) An important piece of information that is missing from biogeographic analyses is how areas were or were not connected over time (present as supplementary files only on Zenodo). In other words, what were your time-stratified models? This is crucial for ARE and BSM analyses. One of the things we were curious about was how India and the Burmese terrane were treated. Also, we do not think we clearly understood what some of the panels in Fig. 3 were showing. For example, in Fig 3A, if we lookt only at the four rightmost bars, we count more than 800 dispersal events near the Miocene/Pliocene boundary, which is colossal. But since this figure is based on 1000 simulations, we think that ‘only’ 80% of the simulations reported a dispersal event at this time, and that 7 bioregions can be the source of this potential dispersal event (even if Indomalaya seems the most likely). Is this correct? In any case, it also means that some of these ‘contemporaneous’ events actually occur in different clades in these simulations. Furthermore, the events are shown every Myr, but the counts were done in sliding windows of 5 (in the Methods) or 10 (in the caption) Myrs. Is there a possibility of overestimating the number of events because of this sliding window? As you can see from our questions, we may have not have understood well what readers should see and take away from this figure. We appreciate that BSM was used to get an idea of the uncertainty in the biogeographic scenario, but we found the results confusing. Would it be worth contrasting these results with the dispersal events found in the ARE analysis? Finally, the readability of Fig. 2B, which also shows the results of dispersal events from the 1000 simulations, could be improved: as it stands, we mainly see the numbers representing the specific richness rather than the dispersal events, whose directions are sometimes obstructed by these numbers.

In addition, we highlight below potential limitations in some of the analyses and recommend additional sensitivity analyses and tests to strengthen the manuscript with regard to phylogenetic inferences (and in particular the potential impact of the grafting approach), datings, biogeographic (and in particular the impact of the controversial +J models) and dating analyses.

*Phylogenetic inferences*
We are concerned about a few points in the methodology used for phylogenetic inference: the number of outgroups; model selection; the limited discussion of the quality of the phylogenetic analyses; and the grafting approach.
6) The authors reconstructed their phylogenetic tree using only three outgroup taxa, namely Paraponera clava (Paraponerinae), Proceratium google (Proceratiinae), and Amblyopone australis (Amblyoponinae). However, previous studies, including some of the co-authors of the present paper, have clearly demonstrated that outgroup choice can affect phylogenetic reconstructions, particularly in ants (Borowiec et al., 2019 - MPE; or Spasojević et al., 2021 although in a total-evidence dating framework). In particular, it remains to be seen how the inclusion of formicoid outgroups or even representatives of the Leptanillinae might affect their results, if at all.
7) The authors used a GTR+F+G4 model in their unpartitioned analyses without justifying this choice. Given that IQ-TREE was used, why not perform a ModelFinder analysis to determine the best model for the unpartitioned analysis (especially since that the authors used it to determine the partitioning scheme and the best model in the partitioned analyses)? A rationale for model selection would strengthen the methodological transparency and reproducibility of the study.
8) There is little discussion of the quality of the phylogenetic analyses, no formal statistical tests are performed, and the uncertainty that short internodes introduce into the results is not addressed, particularly in the ‘Odontomachus-group’ (see Supplementary Figure S3).
9) The authors rely heavily on a grafting approach to supplement their otherwise strong initial sampling. While this practice is common in similar analyses (e.g., Rabosky et al., 2018 - Nature; Economo et al., 2018 - Nat. Commun.) and we do not object to its use, it is important to acknowledge its potential implications. Previous studies have shown that inferring clade-specific evolutionary histories from both grafted and non-grafted phylogenies can have a significant impact on diversification analyses. Given the strong claims presented in this study, we believe this effect warrants further investigation and discussion. At a minimum, the full set of biogeographic and diversification analyses should also be performed on the non-grafted tree, and the results compared to assess the robustness of the conclusions.
10) Since the authors evaluated three different partitioning schemes—unpartitioned, by locus with merging, and Sliding Window Site Characteristics (SWSC) based on entropy with merging—it would be beneficial to include the detailed topologies in the Supplementary Material along with a discussion of their differences. Simply stating that the SWSC analysis yielded the “highest likelihood” to justify prioritizing it over the others does not seem sufficient. The authors should compare the three topologies obtained under different partitioning schemes, and the grafted vs. non-grafted topologies to assess how differences in partitioning and grafting affect divergence time estimates, as these variations are likely to have significant downstream effects on all subsequent analyses.

*Divergence dating*
11) We wonder why some fossils were not used as additional calibrations. We agree that some fossils are dubious, poorly preserved, and cannot be reliably used as calibration points, but ants have one of the best fossil records of the order Hymenoptera, and it is a pity not to take advantage of this. Calibrations strangely overlooked in this manuscript include (not exhaustive):
- a) Platythyrea dlusskyi Aria et al. 2011 from Ypresian Oise amber, which can be used to calibrate the Platythyreini (Aria et al. 2011 - Zootaxa). Given its age and the 95% HDP of the node Platythyreini it is likely that it will push towards slightly older age the node or at least help in reducing the 50 Ma interval of the HDP. It has been used in other studies (e.g., Borowiec et al 2019 - MPE)
- b) Pachycondyla(s) from Baltic amber can be used to calibrate either Pachy + Neo or the crown Pachy, depending on the interpretation you make of their placement, but in both cases they will likely impact the dating (e.g., Dlussky 2009 - Paleontol. J.).
- c) Brachyponera from Zhangpu amber (Wang et al. 2021 - Sci. Adv., see supp material) can be used to calibrate Brachyponera, likely contributing to better estimate the origin of this genus.
Overall, the authors should say a bit more about their rationale for the selection of fossil calibrations in general. Parham et al. (2012 - Syst. Biol.) is a good starting point (we've seen the supplementary file on Zenodo), but it would be helpful to read a bit more about their overall thinking. This might include the otherwise plausible fossils not used, and the reasons for their exclusion.
12) The authors chose to calibrate their tree using MCMCTree applied to a reduced set of taxa, and then scaled it to the full dataset with TreePL. Given the small size of their subsampled dataset and the ongoing advances in dating analyses—particularly regarding the incorporation of fossil data—we wonder why they did not opt for the fossilized birth-death (FBD) process (Stadler 2010 - J. Theor. Biol.; Heath et al. 2014 - PNAS).
FBD-based methods can overcome several limitations associated with node calibration approaches, allowing for the integration of a wider range of fossil data. Given the extensive fossil record of ants and their relatively well-established taxonomic classifications, this method is likely to yield robust results. Alternatively, if the authors are concerned about gaps in the fossil record in certain geological periods, or skeptical about the classical FBD approach, they could use a sequential sampling framework using a birth–death skyline tree prior (BDSS; Stadler et al. 2013 - PNAS; Culshaw et al. 2019 - Evolution). This method allows fossil sampling proportions to be modeled as time-heterogeneous, incorporating time slices before and after the oldest fossil sample using tools such as the TreeSlicer function in the skylinetools package (https://github.com/laduplessis/skylinetools). We strongly encourage the authors to investigate how their methodological choices affect divergence time estimates.
13) Lastly, as emphasized in our point 9), the authors should investigate how divergence time estimates vary between the three different partitioning schemes and provide a thorough discussion of their results. It is well known that dating estimates can vary significantly depending on the methodology, priors, and calibration choices. For a manuscript aiming to elucidate the global diversification and biogeographic history of a clade, the current analyses appear insufficiently comprehensive. Extending these comparisons would strengthen the conclusions of the study and provide a more robust framework for understanding the evolutionary timeline of the Ponerinae, while also serving as a textbook example for future work.

*Historical Biogeography*
14) The authors use BioGeoBEARS 1.1.3 (Matzke 2013 - FoB, 2018) for their biogeographic analyses, and specifically use the DEC+J model (Matzke 2014 - Syst. Biol.). However, they do not provide a clear rationale for selecting DEC+J over the DEC model, other than an AICc comparison. While the authors state that DEC+J was selected as the best-fitting model, it is important to acknowledge the ongoing debate regarding statistical validity and model selection process in BioGeoBEARS (Ree and Sanmartín, 2018 - Syst. Biol.). Additionally, the DEC+J model has been criticized for often yielding null or unrealistically low extinction rates (Sanmartín and Meseguer, 2016 - Front. Genet.) and for favoring direct dispersal over widespread ancestral ranges—an assumption that may not be appropriate for reconstructing the evolutionary history of Ponerinae (Rolland and Condamine, 2019 - J. Biogeogr.). We believe that these concerns can be easily addressed by re-running the analyses using the DEC model. Given the authors’ established analytical pipeline, this should be feasible within a reasonable timeframe. This would not only strengthen the findings of the paper if the results are consistent with the initial analyses, but would also provide valuable insights and discussion in the case of discrepancies.

*Diversification dynamics*
15) The authors refer directly to BAMM in their diversification analyses. BAMM is indeed a powerful tool for inferring extinction and origination rates and can be easily integrated with STRAPP and other downstream analyses. While the BAMM approach can assess diversification rate heterogeneity on highly incomplete and phylogenetically non-random datasets, it has been criticized for identifiability issues (Louca & Pennell, 2020 - Nature). These concerns are significant and have far-reaching implications, as they affect all widely used methods for studying diversification, including those used in this study. We think that a section in the supplementary material discussing how the authors have addressed these issues is mandatory.
16) As with other sections, we feel that the manuscript lacks sufficient sensitivity analyses. We strongly recommend that the authors perform their BAMM analyses on the non-grafted tree as well as on the different topologies obtained under the different partitioning schemes. The results should then be compared and discussed. Given the known sensitivity of BAMM to taxon sampling and tree structure, we would expect the outcomes of these analyses to differ.
17) Why was BAMM chosen over alternative approaches such as ClaDS2 (Maliet et al. 2019 - NEE), LSBDS (Höhna et al. 2019 - bioRxiv), PESTO (Kopperud & Höhna 2023 - https://github.com/kopperud/Pesto.jl), or MTBD (Barido-Sottani et al. 2020 - Syst. Biol.)? The choice of one method over another—while potentially justified—can have a significant impact on estimates of branch-specific diversification rates (Martínez-Gómez et al. 2024 - Evol. Lett.). While we do not expect the authors to repeat all their analyses using multiple methods (as we already suggest several additional analyses), we encourage them to explore ways to cross-validate their results.
Additional visualizations of BAMM outputs would also be beneficial. At the very least, a tree displaying BAMM-derived rates should be included in the supplementary material, along with a figure assessing MCMC convergence for the BAMM run.
We are aware that we have suggested a number of possible additional analyses here, but these are mostly aimed at strengthening the manuscript and better exploring the limits and sensitivity of their results. Finally, we would like to congratulate the authors on their work, which already includes several analyses aimed at better understanding the distribution pattern of Ponerinae.

Minor comments:
· L 98: Kachin amber from Myanmar (Late Cretaceous: 94-100 My)
Radiometric data established an early Cenomanian age (98.79 ± 0.62 Ma) for Kachin amber, based on zircons from volcanic clasts found within the amber-bearing sediments (Shi et al. 2012 - Cret. Res.). Some ammonites found in the amber-bearing bed and within amber corroborate a late Albian–early Cenomanian age (Cruickshank & Ko 2003 - J. Asian Earth Sci.).
· L 197: “we designed a custom screening procedure to detect bioregional outliers and removed dubious records falling in rarely documented bioregions”
How many dubious records and bioregions are we talking about?
· L 305-307: This estimate falls within the range of previous estimates and dates the emergence of the extant ponerine ant clade during the Early Cretaceous, coinciding with the timing of origins of other ant subfamilies.
This sentence is not correct. The range is not in agreement with the ages from a few recent and older studies: 73 (61–84) in Borowiec et al. (2019 - MPE) or 56–60 in Moreau and Bell (2013 - Evolution).
· L 427: How many diversification shifts were identified in your BAMM analysis, and where are they located on the phylogenetic tree?
· L. 443: Is the RNW value correct? (seems wrong when compared to Fig. 5A)
· The authors seem to equate in-situ diversification with endemism, which are two very different concepts. A few sentences of the manuscript should be rephrased accordingly.

### Reviewer 2

Dear Editor,

In their manuscript "Timing is everything: Evolution of ponerine ants highlights how dispersal history shapes modern biodiversity" Doré et al. present the results of a thorough phylogeny-based analysis of the global historical biogeography of ants in the subfamily Ponerinae.

For their study, the authors first reconstructed phylogenetic relationships and divergence times among 789 ponerine species and morphospecies using phylogenomic data. Then, they grafted missing species on the tree based on taxonomic background data, to obtain a "full" 1534-tip tree for ponerine ants. The main analyses are based on the best full dated tree as well as 1000 posterior "full" trees sampled for estimating the effects of phylogenetic uncertainty. The authors then estimated ancestral geographic ranges across the fossil-calibrated trees based on an extensive global database of the distributions of extant ponerine species. These ancestral reconstructions are combined with phylogeny-based inferences of diversification rates in past and present lineages, to infer support for three different hypotheses on the distribution of species diversity observed in the group today. The main conclusion is that the latitudinal gradient seen in the diversity of extant ponerine ants is mainly the result of a tendency to remain in the ancestral tropical habitat (tropical niche conservatism), while asymmetric dispersal and differences in diversification rates have a minor role. The results are discussed in relation to diversity patterns found in other taxa.

I find the study highly interesting and impressive. The breadth of phylogenetic and statistical methods covered by the work is breathtaking, but Supplementary figures S1 and S2 do a good job in explaining how the phylogenetic and biogeographic datasets used in the different analyses were compiled.

I might have commented on the restriction to net diversification rates and the existence of megathermal forests in the northern Hemisphere during the early Cenozoic, but both of these issues are in fact dealt with in the end of the Discussion. These challenges are by no means restricted to this study, and I find the caveats given in the text sufficient.

I cannot claim to be a specialist in all aspects of the highly diverse statistical analyses, but the methods used in the parts that I have experience with seem to be up to date, logical and justified. In some cases, there would be alternative methods available, but these are not necessarily better than the ones used here. The combined analyses and plots of results from different statistical methods are highly innovative. To me it seems that such approaches might be of use also in fields not directly related to biogeography.

Based on the importance of the results and high quality of the data and analyses of the study, I recommend publication of the manuscript as-is. The supplementary information and scripts and data files in databases appear to contain all information necessary for replicating the analyses and results. The manuscript package is so carefully prepared that I struggled to find even small mistakes or typos from the text, these are listed below.

Minor comments:
R40: drivers -> driver?
R59: "by using"?
R67: Split paragraph before "The"?
R113: "that" -> ", which"?
R165: 2 x "in"
Figure 3: Is "Sources" the correct word in (E) and (F)?
R579: "Ponerine" -> "Ponerines"
- The "Wilcox test" is mentioned in the text and supplementary methods, I believe this should be spelled out as "Wilcoxon test" when used in text?
- In the Supplementary information, one sentence seems to be essentially repeated twice in the Phylogenetic inference section: "Among the three partitioning schemes, the SWSC-En with merging scheme had the highest likelihood and was selected as the best result for downstream analyses. Among the three partitioning schemes, the SWSC with merging scheme had the highest log-likelihood and was selected as the best result for downstream analyses (unpartitioned: -37.82 × 106, by locus with merging: -37.30 × 106, SWSC-EN with merging: -37.08 × 106)."
- In the Reporting Summary, the Reporting on sex section contains the sentence "Sex-based analyses are not required for this type of phylogenomic study as no sex-linked loci were studied." Here it could be specified that ants (and other hymenopterans) have a haplodiploid sex determination system, so sex-linked loci technically do not exist.

One of the things we were curious about was how India and the Burmese terrane were treated.
As the reviewers noted, this piece of information is available in the Supplementary Data under
the Supplementary Table S7 with all associated references used to define the connectivity
over time of the bioregions used in our study. We now also provide this information as a
Supplementary Table (Table S7 in ‘Supplementary Data S1-S7.xlsx’) directly accessible
from the online version of the article.
Because our downstream analyses rely on comparing in situ diversification dynamics and
dispersal pathways between bioregions, we opted to use a geographic classification with
bioregions of comparable areas to limit bias due to size differences. Moreover, the vast
majority of ponerines found in the present-day Burmese area and in the Indian subcontinent
are also encroaching on the surrounding South-Asian regions, thereby limiting greatly the
informative power of historical biogeographic inferences treating those areas as separate
entities. Therefore, we classified India and the Burmese terrane under a joint IndoMalayan
bioregion, even though those territories had a partly independent geological history. For similar
reasons, we decided to keep Madagascar as part of Afrotropics. These choices are in-line
with both historical and recent studies of similar scope aiming to produce bioregional
schemes at global scale, or to reconstruct the biogeographic history of cosmopolitan diverse
clades (Wallace, 1876; Udvardy, 1975; Rueda et al., 2013; Chazot et al., 2021; Reginato et
al., 2022; Kawahara et al., 2023).
Following the reviewers’ legitimate concerns, we now elaborate to a wider extent on this
rationale in the Supplementary Methods (see Section 7.1 on Bioregion scheme).

*Phylogenetic inferences*
We are concerned about a few points in the methodology used for phylogenetic inference: the
number of outgroups; model selection; the limited discussion of the quality of the phylogenetic
analyses; and the grafting approach.
6) The authors reconstructed their phylogenetic tree using only three outgroup taxa, namely
Paraponera clava (Paraponerinae), Proceratium google (Proceratiinae), and Amblyopone
australis (Amblyoponinae). However, previous studies, including some of the co-authors of the
present paper, have clearly demonstrated that outgroup choice can affect phylogenetic
reconstructions, particularly in ants (Borowiec et al., 2019 - MPE; or Spasojević et al., 2021
although in a total-evidence dating framework). In particular, it remains to be seen how the
inclusion of formicoid outgroups or even representatives of the Leptanillinae might affect their
results, if at all.
All molecular phylogenetic studies, going back to 2006, have consistently provided a strong
support for the monophyly of Ponerinae and the reciprocal monophyly of two subclades
(Platythyrea versus all others) at the base of the Ponerinae tree (Brady et al., 2006; Moreau
et al., 2006; Schmidt, 2013; Branstetter et al., 2017; Borowiec et al., 2019, 2025). The
uncertainties in ant phylogeny lie in older splits between subfamilies of poneroids and
formicoids. As pointed out by the reviewers, these uncertainties, which were the focus of a
previous study conducted by some of the authors (Borowiec et al., 2019), do not pertain to the
internal topology of Ponerinae. Therefore, the addition of more outgroups is extremely
unlikely to affect any of our analyses and results, which focus uniquely on this stable
portion of the phylogenetic tree.
Conversely, we chose to follow the most recent best practices in phylogenomics outlined in a
recent study from DeSalle et al., 2023. Here, the authors showed that the former standard
practice of using multiple outgroups often causes random rooting that generates spurious
incongruences in phylogenetic inferences. Instead, they recommended using a single (most
closely) related relative as the outgroup. In our case, we decided to limit our selection of
outgroups to three taxa as adding more outgroups in an already computational-heavy
dataset would not be helpful to achieve our aims and would not provide any additional
insights on the internal evolutionary dynamics of Ponerinae, which is the focus of our study.

7) The authors used a GTR+F+G4 model in their unpartitioned analyses without justifying this
choice. Given that IQ-TREE was used, why not perform a ModelFinder analysis to determine
the best model for the unpartitioned analysis (especially since that the authors used it to
determine the partitioning scheme and the best model in the partitioned analyses)? A rationale
for model selection would strengthen the methodological transparency and reproducibility of
the study.
We selected GTR+F+G4 for the unpartitioned analysis for several reasons. One practical
reason is that performing model selection on unpartitioned, genome-scale datasets using
ModelFinder in IQ-Tree takes an incredibly long time due to the size of the dataset and the
number of models available to test. We chose here to select analyses that would be
efficient while not jeopardizing quality. For similar reasons, all tree inference programs
employ heuristics to search only part of tree space rather than to evaluate all possible
topologies, because the latter is impractical. Similarly, when the SWSC-EN method was first
published, it would output an input file for ParitionFinder2 that restricted the merging model to
GTR+G only. This was done to make the analyses feasible and because of point two below.
Second, GTR is a general, flexible substitution model that allows to parametrize all types of
substitutions and encompasses simpler models as special cases. Given the large size of our
molecular dataset, there is no risk of overparameterization associated with poor parameter
estimation. In this context, directly applying a complex model like GTR+F+G4, for an analysis
with an unpartitioned scheme, is justified and avoids unnecessary model selection steps,
especially since it would converge on simpler models if the data supported it. This choice is
fully in-line with the recommendations of Abadi et al., 2019, who showed in a test study that,
across their simulated datasets, the proportion of correctly inferred tree topologies for the
parameter-rich GTR+I+G model is highly similar to the ones obtained with a model selection
process. They concluded that “there is no clear benefit for performing a model selection
step for phylogeny inference, and a fixed parameter-rich model can be used instead”.
Finally, we analyzed the unpartitioned matrix primarily to see how partitioning could improve
model fit and potentially the phylogenetic results. The two additional partitioning schemes that
we employed, by-locus + merging and SWSC-EN + merging, both did model merging using
GTR+G for merging, followed by full model selection on the final partitioning scheme. Given
that we performed a merging step, it is completely feasible that ModelFinder could have
merged all of the initial by-locus and SWSC partitions back into a single partition, but this did
not occur. Thus, there is no evidence that the unpartitioned analysis is in any way the
ideal partitioning scheme and that is why, in complement with the comparison of likelihoods
and node support values (see Point #10), we selected the phylogeny obtained from the
SWSC-EN + merging scheme as the best tree to conduct downstream analyses.
We now clearly explain this rationale in the dedicated section of the Supplementary Methods
(Section 3. Phylogenetic Inferences), improving methodological transparency and ensuring
perfect reproducibility.

9) The authors rely heavily on a grafting approach to supplement their otherwise strong initial
sampling. While this practice is common in similar analyses (e.g., Rabosky et al., 2018 -
Nature; Economo et al., 2018 - Nat. Commun.) and we do not object to its use, it is important
to acknowledge its potential implications. Previous studies have shown that inferring clade-
specific evolutionary histories from both grafted and non-grafted phylogenies can have a
significant impact on diversification analyses. Given the strong claims presented in this study,
we believe this effect warrants further investigation and discussion. At a minimum, the full set
of biogeographic and diversification analyses should also be performed on the non-grafted
tree, and the results compared to assess the robustness of the conclusions.
We thank the reviewers for highlighting this important methodological choice in our analytical
workflow that led us to elaborate in even more depth the rationale behind this choice. We
argued here that we carefully selected the best suited approach for our type of data and
objectives, that we already included uncertainty in grafting in our downstream analyses
to the maximum extent possible for a reasonable computation-time, and that the use of
alternative approaches based on non-grafted trees would only lead to biased results of lesser
quality than what we have already done and would be improper as sensitivity analyses aiming
to increase the robustness of our results.
We decided to rely on a grafting approach to supplement our initial sampling because
downstream analyses of diversity dynamics based on imputed exhaustive phylogenies have
increased power and lower estimation bias for identifying regime shifts relative to analyses
that use sampling fractions to account for missing taxa (Chang et al., 2020). Moreover,
performing diversification analyses on non-grafted trees would imply a choice between two
equally problematic approaches. (1) We could use a global sampling fraction to account for
the missing taxa. This is highly likely to lead to biased results as the location of missing grafted
taxa in our phylogeny is widely heterogeneous across clades (see Supplementary Figure
S6) and thus will not be reflected with the use of a global sampling fraction parameter
assuming a homogeneous distribution of missing taxa (Cusimano & Renner, 2010; Höhna et
al., 2011). (2) Alternatively, we could use clade-specific sampling fractions to account for the
appropriate number of missing taxa within each subclade. However, this approach has been
pointed to lead to potentially incorrect likelihood calculation behavior (Beaulieu, 2020 -
Vignette in hisse R package: “The problem with clade-specific sampling fractions”, Moore et
al., 2016) and to have low power to appropriately estimate diversification models and
parameters when they fall below 50% (FitzJohn et al. 2009), which would be our case for some
of our clades . Therefore, we followed the recommended approach by the authors of the
BAMM software (http://bamm-project.org/advanced.html; accessed on April 16th, 2025.
Section 9.1 Accounting for non-random incomplete taxon sampling in diversification studies)
that consists in using taxonomically informed grafted trees with missing speciation events
estimated from birth-death models fit on incomplete subclades such as in the TACT method
(Chang et al., 2020) and as described in our own Supplementary Methods (Section 5. Tree
grafting). We now elaborate more thoroughly on this rationale in the dedicated section of the
Supplementary Methods to enhance transparency in our choices of analytic pipeline.

10) Since the authors evaluated three different partitioning schemes—unpartitioned, by locus

We believe that SWSC-EN with model selection and partition merging is the most
sophisticated and appropriate way to partition UCE data. It handles the expected different
evolutionary dynamics occurring in the ultra-conserved and variation section of each locus
and because it starts with a scheme that has each locus split into three distinct partitions and
works its way down towards progressively more merged schemes (Tagliacollo & Lanfear,
2018). This way, unpartitioned and partitioned by-locus schemes are nested within the
SWCS-EN model. In other words, the partition merging step of the SWSC-EN approach would
lead to an unpartitioned or a partitioned by-locus scheme, if one of these received more
statistical support for a given dataset. Thus, beyond the higher likelihood, there is a strong
statistical rationale to select the SWSC-EN approach over the unpartitioned scheme or
the by-locus scheme for downstream analyses. Moreover, the SWSC-EN scheme also
provided the highest node support values with mean UFBS scores of 97.95% vs. 97.48% for
‘unpartitioned’, and 97.84% for ‘by locus with merging. For clarity, we now detail the rationale
for the selection of the best partitioning scheme (See sections in Phylogenetic Inferences in
Main text (L. 172-177) and Supplementary Methods), provide visuals of the phylogenies
resulting from other partitioning schemes and report on the very limited variation that
occurs between them. Indeed, the three partitioning schemes led to highly similar topologies,
with respectively five clades (unpartitioned: 99.4% identity) and one clade (by locus: 99.9%
identity) differing from the SWSC-EN topology due to uncertain placement of single isolated
rogue taxa (see Supplementary Figure S4). We are highly confident that these minor
discrepancies cannot affect our overall conclusions to any detectable degree, comforting our
choice to focus our time-consuming downstream analyses on the best partitioning scheme.

*Divergence dating*
11) We wonder why some fossils were not used as additional calibrations. We agree that some
fossils are dubious, poorly preserved, and cannot be reliably used as calibration points, but
ants have one of the best fossil records of the order Hymenoptera, and it is a pity not to take
advantage of this. Calibrations strangely overlooked in this manuscript include (not
exhaustive):
- a) Platythyrea dlusskyi Aria et al. 2011 from Ypresian Oise amber, which can be used to
calibrate the Platythyreini (Aria et al. 2011 - Zootaxa). Given its age and the 95% HDP of the
node Platythyreini it is likely that it will push towards slightly older age the node or at least help
in reducing the 50 Ma interval of the HDP. It has been used in other studies (e.g., Borowiec et
al 2019 - MPE)
- b) Pachycondyla(s) from Baltic amber can be used to calibrate either Pachy + Neo or the
crown Pachy, depending on the interpretation you make of their placement, but in both cases
they will likely impact the dating (e.g., Dlussky 2009 - Paleontol. J.).
- c) Brachyponera from Zhangpu amber (Wang et al. 2021 - Sci. Adv., see supp material) can
be used to calibrate Brachyponera, likely contributing to better estimate the origin of this
genus.
Overall, the authors should say a bit more about their rationale for the selection of fossil
calibrations in general. Parham et al. (2012 - Syst. Biol.) is a good starting point (we've seen
the supplementary file on Zenodo), but it would be helpful to read a bit more about their overall
thinking. This might include the otherwise plausible fossils not used, and the reasons for their
exclusion.
We thank the reviewers for the attention they have given our divergence dating approaches.
We have altered the text in Supplementary Methods to make our reasoning more explicit
(see Section 4 - Divergence dating). Our guiding principles for choosing fossil node
calibrations were:
1) Only using fossils that could be confidently assigned to crown groups.
2) We conservatively assumed that each fossil could belong to either the crown or stem group
of a clade in which it has been placed in the literature, except for those that had been explicitly
placed using total-evidence tip dating (Ronquist et al., 2012).
3) When multiple fossils of the same age informed a set of nested nodes, we chose to calibrate
only the shallowest node, assuming the fossil to bracket the minimum age for that node.
These are common guiding principles in node calibration divergence dating analyses,
successfully applied in ants and Hymenoptera by the authors and others before (e.g, Peters
et al. 2017, Blaimer et al. 2023, Borowiec et al. 2025, and others). This results in seven fossils
identified as relevant for this study. The importance of the first and second guiding principles
is well-articulated in the reviewer-cited Parham et al. 2012. The third principle is simply to
avoid redundant constraints on dependent events. Consider a tree (A,(B,C)) calibrated with
Baltic Amber fossils at both the MRCAs of BC and ABC. In this case, these nodes are nested,
AB is by definition younger than the ancestor of ABC, and so it makes no sense for both to
have the same minimum age.
With these in mind, we can address the individual fossils mentioned by the reviewers. We
actually considered the fossil Platythyrea. However, because it is impossible to deduce
whether this fossil is within the crown group of this genus, it would have to calibrate the split
between Platythyreini and Ponerini (i.e., the rest of Ponerinae). For this initial split, however,
we chose a much older (minimum 94 Ma) undescribed species of Ponerinae that was explicitly
placed as sister to Ponerini using many morphological characters obtained for total-evidence
dating by Boudinot et al. 2022.
The multiple species of fossil Pachycondyla have all been described prior to the recognition
the genus was polyphyletic, leading to its split into 19 different genera in 2014 (Schmidt and
Shattuck, 2014). It is beyond the scope of this paper to comprehensively re-evaluate these
fossils. Some of these had apparently been examined by the authors of the generic revision,
with the outcome being the following statement (Schmidt and Shattuck, 2014, p. 155):
“We have not managed to discern the proper taxonomic placement for a handful of ponerine
species previously associated with Pachycondyla. In some cases, this uncertainty stems from
our failure to examine specimens of the species in question (especially when the original
descriptions are ambiguous), while in other cases the morphological traits of the species leave
doubts about its affinities. We leave these species as incertae sedis within Pachycondyla while
acknowledging this placement is undoubtedly incorrect. Exact placement will require detailed
examination of relevant material of these taxa.”
The fossil Brachyponera from Wang et al. 2021 was not included because it contradicts some
of the recommendations of Parham et al. 2012: It has not been officially described as a species
and is mentioned in the supplement without any identifying characters and no photograph
available for examination. We opted instead to calibrate the next node down with a much more
completely described and unmistakable fossil of the same age, Odontoponera
pseudotransversa (Perrichot, 2022).
We were aware of and considered in this study fossil data from Jouault et al. (2025) and
Jouault et al. (2024). We chose not to use fossils reported only in supplementary data files,
especially when they lacked formal taxonomic descriptions, accessible supporting images, or
clear character justification. To do otherwise would contradict best practices outlined by
Parham et al. 2012.
We believe that our selection of fossil calibrations is as complete as possible when
following best practices for node calibration and our rationale above, supported by the
cited literature. Combined with root prior spanning 80 Ma around the dates recovered in the
literature (see Supplementary Information Section 4 - Divergence Dating) and 1000
posterior trees used in downstream analyses, our conclusions are more robust to
uncertainty in dating analyses than the literature standard in macroevolutionary
studies, which often consider only a single “best” tree.
We thank the reviewers for the prompt to explain our rationale, which we do by adding the
following to the Supplementary Information (in Section 4. Divergence dating):
“We selected fossil calibrations following three guiding principles: (1) fossils had to be
confidently assignable to total groups; (2) in the absence of total-evidence phylogenetic
placement, we conservatively assumed that fossils could belong to either stem or crown
groups; and (3) when multiple fossils of similar age could inform a set of nested nodes, we
calibrated only the shallowest such node to avoid redundant constraints. These principles
were applied in conjunction with best practices outlined by Parham et al. (2012) for fossil
selection and have been applied successfully in divergence dating of ants and other
Hymenoptera (e.g., Peters et al. 2017, Borowiec et al. 2025, Blaimer et al. 2023). Following
this approach, we identified seven fossil calibrations appropriate for our analyses, prioritizing
those with clear morphological justification, sufficient preservation, and unambiguous
taxonomic placement.”

12) The authors chose to calibrate their tree using MCMCTree applied to a reduced set of
taxa, and then scaled it to the full dataset with TreePL. Given the small size of their
subsampled dataset and the ongoing advances in dating analyses—particularly regarding the
incorporation of fossil data—we wonder why they did not opt for the fossilized birth-death
(FBD) process (Stadler 2010 - J. Theor. Biol.; Heath et al. 2014 - PNAS).
FBD-based methods can overcome several limitations associated with node calibration
approaches, allowing for the integration of a wider range of fossil data. Given the extensive
fossil record of ants and their relatively well-established taxonomic classifications, this method
is likely to yield robust results. Alternatively, if the authors are concerned about gaps in the
fossil record in certain geological periods, or skeptical about the classical FBD approach, they
could use a sequential sampling framework using a birth–death skyline tree prior (BDSS;
Stadler et al. 2013 - PNAS; Culshaw et al. 2019 - Evolution). This method allows fossil
sampling proportions to be modeled as time-heterogeneous, incorporating time slices before
and after the oldest fossil sample using tools such as the TreeSlicer function in the skylinetools
package (https://github.com/laduplessis/skylinetools). We strongly encourage the authors to
investigate how their methodological choices affect divergence time estimates.
We thank the authors for this suggestion and would like to respond by explaining our rationale
for not using fossilized birth-death (FBD) methods. We believe that there are a number of
trade-offs using classical node calibrations versus FBD-based methods, and that the goals
of our study were already fully accomplished by node dating.
First, the use of FBD is much more computationally intensive. We know from experience
that in order to apply the FBD framework we would have had to decrease the number of loci
used dramatically, even in reduced dataset, perhaps to the order of 5-10 loci for the analysis
to converge in a reasonable time. Furthermore, our reduced dataset would have to include
much more taxa to accommodate all the nodes that need to be constrained to place additional
potential fossils. Because we perceive the completeness of our data in terms of taxa
represented by genomic data as a major strength and innovation of this study (nearly half of
all species represented by UCE data), we decided it would have been undesirable to reduce
the dataset to a tiny fraction of loci just to use FBD.
Furthermore, while FBD can theoretically offer greater accuracy, it often has low precision
relative to node dating (e.g., Heath et al. 2014, Borowiec 2019). Since absolute time
divergence estimates vary so widely in the ant systematic literature (Borowiec et al. 2020,
Borowiec et al. 2025), we focused primarily on the robustness of our analyses regarding
divergence time ranges from classical node calibrations. As mentioned above, we were able
to inject considerable uncertainty into our dating by applying broad root prior encompassing
the ranges from published studies. This way, we are already generating a wide range of
scenarios that could have been produced by FBD without using explicit morphological
placement of fossils that may sometimes introduce additional bias. We believe this makes our
conclusions robust and less dependent on the many assumptions inherently present in
divergence dating, whether using FBD or node dating.
We are not particularly concerned about the limitations of FBD-based approaches and believe
that it would have been advantageous under certain circumstances. A major advantage of
FBD is the possibility of explicit placement of fossils using morphological data in a total-
evidence framework (cf. Ronquist et al. 2012, Boudinot et al. 2022). If a comprehensive
morphological matrix from all extant and fossil ponerines was available for this project, we
would have chosen FBD. As it is, we generated great amounts of molecular data for this
project and decided to prioritize information therein.
We hope the reviewers appreciate this rationale and realize that it would have been both
computationally challenging to carry out FBD for our dataset and an enormous burden to
repeat all our downstream analyses for potentially limited improvement (see for instance
Beaulieu & O’Meara 2023).

As outlined in our response to Point #3, we believe that we have taken a special and, to our
knowledge, unprecedented care in addressing uncertainties in divergence dating (and
taxonomic grafting) down to the selection of biogeographic models and estimates of ancestral
ranges (Supplementary Information Tables S4 & S8). While we appreciate the suggestion
to extend sensitivity analyses further, the reviewers should notice that we are already
computationally not able to carry on the multiplication of sensitivity analyses further
down our analytic pipeline in a reasonable time, knowing that the Biogeographic Stochastic
Mapping, Dispersal events summaries across time sliding-windows, BAMM diversification
analyses, STRAPP tests over evolutionary time, RISR investigations, and investigation of
lineage origins over time already require over a week of CPU-time for a single
phylogenetic hypothesis.
Nonetheless, we fully acknowledge the importance of testing the robustness of our main
conclusions to dating uncertainty and have worked to address this to the greatest extent
possible while keeping the analytic pipeline under a feasible, albeit already massive
computational and time burden. To this end, we performed the entire pipeline of
downstream analyses using the two most extreme hypotheses for divergence dating
supported by our data (i.e., using the youngest and oldest divergence age estimates found
among our posterior samples). We tested for correlations between the net diversification rates
estimated from BAMM for each hypothesis and found significant positive relationships
(Spearman’s rank correlation: MCC vs. Youngest: ρ = 0.619, t = 13.7, df = 303, p < 0.001;
MCC vs. Oldest: ρ = 0.904, t = 37.4, df = 313, p < 0.001; Supplementary Figs. S14 & S15).
In complement, we also found high agreements in the ancestral range estimates across the
divergence dating hypotheses with Cohen’s Kappa indices higher than 0.90 (MCC vs.
Youngest = 0.971; MCC vs. Oldest = 0.907) reflected by the high similarity in ancestral ranges
mapped on the respective phylogenies (Fig. 1; Supplementary Fig. S9).
We now show that our main conclusions regarding the prevalence of colonization timing
(TfAH) over differences in diversification rates (DRH) and asymmetry in dispersal flux
(ADH) in explaining present-day biodiversity patterns in ponerine ants are robust
regardless of the hypothesis for divergence dating selected (see new Supplementary
Figures S9, S11, S12, S13, S15, S17, S19, S22 & S23, and Supplementary Tables S2, S3,
S6 & S7; and additions to the Main text: L. 192-194, 203-205, 251, 255-260, 281-283, 361-
364, 369-370, 432-437, 487-492, 505-510, 538-543, 553-555, 623-626 & 663). Those
sensitivity analyses also emphasize that the relative timing of colonization events across
bioregions is the key factor, independently from the absolute estimated timing of events.
We are confident that, thanks to the addition of those new sensitivity analyses in complement
to the original ones, we now provide a fully transparent, robust, and extensive analytical
framework that will likely contribute to establishing a new standard for future large-scale
macroevolutionary studies.
*Historical Biogeography*
14) The authors use BioGeoBEARS 1.1.3 (Matzke 2013 - FoB, 2018) for their biogeographic
analyses, and specifically use the DEC+J model (Matzke 2014 - Syst. Biol.). However, they
do not provide a clear rationale for selecting DEC+J over the DEC model, other than an AICc
comparison. While the authors state that DEC+J was selected as the best-fitting model, it is
important to acknowledge the ongoing debate regarding statistical validity and model selection
process in BioGeoBEARS (Ree and Sanmartín, 2018 - Syst. Biol.). Additionally, the DEC+J
model has been criticized for often yielding null or unrealistically low extinction rates
(Sanmartín and Meseguer, 2016 - Front. Genet.) and for favoring direct dispersal over
widespread ancestral ranges—an assumption that may not be appropriate for reconstructing
the evolutionary history of Ponerinae (Rolland and Condamine, 2019 - J. Biogeogr.). We
believe that these concerns can be easily addressed by re-running the analyses using the
DEC model. Given the authors’ established analytical pipeline, this should be feasible within
a reasonable timeframe. This would not only strengthen the findings of the paper if the results
are consistent with the initial analyses, but would also provide valuable insights and discussion
in the case of discrepancies.
We are aware of the debates in the community surrounding the use of the +J models including
jump dispersal at speciation for biogeographic inferences. We do not think it is the purpose of
our study to reopen this discussion, but we agree with the reviewers that potential bias
associated with the use of specific models should be acknowledged. To our view, the
issue of model selection has been convincingly addressed by the author of the BioGeoBEARS
meta-model himself in his reply to Ree and Sanmartín’s concerns (Matzke, 2022). Here, he
exposed how the likelihood-based comparison framework commonly accepted as the
standard in modern statistics (Burnham, & Anderson, 2002), including comparison of
macroevolutionary models of trait evolution, SSE models, and partitioning scheme for
phylogenetic inferences (see Point #10) is a valid approach to model selection (Harmon,
2019). DEC and DEC+J are effectively both special cases of a ClaSSE model relying on a
similar framework for likelihood definition. Moreover, the DEC model is nested within the
DEC+J model which implies that direct comparison of model fit and parameter estimates
are valid and easily accessible. The selection of biogeographic models based on AICc
comparison, especially within the BioGeoBEARS framework, is currently the common best
practice used by high-impact studies involving biogeographic analyses of similar scope (Klein
et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2022; Weil et al., 2023; Leong et al., 2025). In our case, the statistical
support for DEC+J over DEC is overwhelming with 1000 out of 1000 of our posterior trees
accounting for both uncertainty in divergence dating and in taxon grafting leading to the
selection of the DEC+J model over DEC, DIVALIKE, and DIVALIKE+J models using AICc as
a selection criterion (Supplementary Information Table S2).
As stated by the reviewers, an important point of contention against the use of DEC+J models
is the fact that it often yields unrealistically low extinction rates and limited residence times in
widespread areas by allowing jump-dispersal at speciation ((A) → (A),(B)) as an alternative
mechanism to range expansion ((A) → (AB)) followed by a vicariance ((AB) → (A),(B)) or a
sympatric subset speciation event ((AB) → (AB),(B)) that both require a temporary widespread
state to model a cladogenetic range transition (Sanmartín and Meseguer, 2016). While these
criticisms are valid, the use of a DEC model that does not allow jump-dispersal events to
occur may also entail equally, if not even more, problematic assumptions in the context
of a time-stratified model. Indeed, under the DEC model, in a time-stratified context using
adjacency matrices to control for the validity of widespread ranges (AB) during geological
periods based on connectivity between terrestrial landmasses, no transition (A → B) is possible
between non-adjacent areas because all succession of events modeling such transition
require an invalid temporary wide-spread state (AB). Therefore, a time-stratified DEC model
is mechanically denying the possibility of long-dispersal events followed by isolation leading
to speciation (i.e., a founder event) between two non-adjacent areas. Conversely, under a
time-stratified DEC+J model, such events, especially on a geological timescale, are exactly
accounted for by jump-dispersals that describe a range transition associated with speciation
((A) → (A),(B)). Long-distance dispersal events across non-adjacent areas are to be expected
for ants which managed for instance to colonize remote Pacific islands (e.g., Lucky & Sarnat,
2010). Using dispersal multiplier matrices (+W models) would not solve this issue as they only
modulate dispersal parameter values, but do not affect the state space, and in particular do
not make widespread ranges available for transitions between non-adjacent areas in DEC
models.
Overall, we recognize that there may be potentially problematic biases with the DEC+J model,
but we stress here that different problematic assumptions are also associated with DEC
models. We now explicitly acknowledge the possible biases of the DEC+J model in the
Supplementary Methods (Section 7.2 Ancestral Range Estimates with BioGeoBEARS).
However, we believe our current model selection framework is grounded on compelling
statistical support and aligns with the current best practice in biogeographic inferences
and statistics in general. Given the unambiguous and robust statistical support for the
DEC+J model over the DEC model found with our dataset, we believe it is appropriate to
proceed with the DEC+J model in our analytical pipeline. While we understand the concerns
surrounding the use of DEC+J, we feel that disregarding the result of our carefully designed
model selection process, including time-consuming sensitivity analyses that go already
beyond any practice in the field, would undermine the evidence-based approach we aim to
promote in this study.

*Diversification dynamics*
15) The authors refer directly to BAMM in their diversification analyses. BAMM is indeed a
powerful tool for inferring extinction and origination rates and can be easily integrated with
STRAPP and other downstream analyses. While the BAMM approach can assess
diversification rate heterogeneity on highly incomplete and phylogenetically non-random
datasets, it has been criticized for identifiability issues (Louca & Pennell, 2020 - Nature). These
concerns are significant and have far-reaching implications, as they affect all widely used
methods for studying diversification, including those used in this study. We think that a section
in the supplementary material discussing how the authors have addressed these issues is
mandatory.
We thank the reviewers for raising this important point. We fully acknowledge the identifiability
issues discussed by Louca & Pennell (2020), who showed that under generalized birth–death
models, multiple distinct diversification scenarios with time-varying speciation and extinction
rates can yield identical likelihoods for a given extant timetree. These concerns have indeed
major implications for the interpretation of diversification analyses and merit transparent
discussion. We present here, and in the dedicated section of Supplementary Information
(Section 8.2 BAMM diversification rates), the different steps taken in our analytic framework
in order to mitigate potential detrimental effects of those identifiability issues on our
conclusions.
As a preamble, it is worth noting, as the reviewers did, that these identifiability challenges
are not specific to BAMM, but apply equally to all currently available diversification methods
that model time-varying speciation and extinction rates from extant phylogenies, including
alternative approaches such as ClaDS2, LSBDS, PESTO, or MTBD. To our knowledge, all
such methods operate within the same general modeling framework of generalized birth–
death models and are thus subject to the same theoretical constraints.
(1) We focused our analyses on net diversification rates rather than on the absolute estimation
of speciation and extinction rates individually. While net diversification is also affected by
identifiability issues, it is generally more robust and interpretable than attempting to
disentangle speciation and extinction trends independently (as noted by Louca & Pennell).
(2) We relied on a Bayesian framework (BAMM) to estimate changes in diversification rates
over time and clades. Even though not perfect, the sampling approach of Bayesian methods
allows theoretically to sample multiple of the infinite congruent diversification histories that can
lead to similar likelihood, effectively accounting for a portion of the uncertainty regarding
the identification of the “best” fitting diversification history. We carried on this uncertainty
down to our tests for diversification rate differences as we performed STRAPP tests that are
especially designed to be run across posterior samples from a BAMM encompassing a
diversity of alternative diversification histories.
(3) The set of diversification histories that yield similarly maximized likelihood is called a
“congruence class”. Such a congruence class contains exactly one model with a complete
sampling fraction (ρ = 1) and absence of extinctions (μ = 0). This model presents speciation
rates equal to the ‘pulled speciation rates’ defined by Louca & Pennell as the key parameter
identifiable from time-varying BD models and suggested to be used for further interpretation.
Since we used grafted trees (effectively having a complete sampling fraction), and obtained
extinction estimates that were relatively low compared to speciation rates (mean μ = 0.041;
mean λ = 0.148), the net diversification rates we used for downstream analyses are actually
somewhat close to the ‘pulled speciation rates’ defined by Louca & Pennell (and arguably
largely ignored by the community of macroevolutionists ever since).
(4) As exposed in more details in our reply to Point #17, we combined different approaches
(BAMM vs Regional In-Situ Radiation analyses vs GeoSSE) in an attempt to cross
validate our results following the framework introduced by Chazot et al., 2021.
We believe the diversification analyses we present in this study, especially when paired with
alternative approaches and conservative interpretation limited to net diversification rates,
remain informative and methodologically sound despite the challenges raised by Louca &
Pennell. Following the reviewer’s recommendation, we have now included a dedicated
paragraph in the Supplementary Methods (Section 8.2 BAMM diversification rates), where
we explicitly discuss these theoretical limitations and clarify the rationale for our
methodological choices accordingly.
