We favored the use of BAMM to carry out diversification analyses as, as noted by the
reviewers, it is easily integrated with the STRAPP tests we performed in downstream
analyses. This choice is motivated by the adequation of BAMM outputs with the type of
tests and analyses we aimed to perform for this study. Beyond facilitating the use of
STRAPP tests, BAMM also allowed us to carry out the uncertainty of diversification histories
in downstream analyses such as the estimation of the evolution of rates through times (Fig.
5), and the mapping of longitudinal and latitudinal gradients of diversification rates
(Supplementary Figure S9). We are aware of the existence of the alternative approaches
listed by the reviewers, but as noted by Reviewer #2: “there would be alternative methods
available, but these are not necessarily better than the ones used here.”. It is beyond the
scope of this study to compare the multiple methods existing to produce the type of
diversification analyses included as a key step in our analytic pipeline, especially in a
context of a study dealing with large datasets incurring thousands of CPU-hours of
computation. To our knowledge, the standard for recent studies with similar scope is to rely
on BAMM for diversification analyses and sometimes DR statistics to quickly estimate tip-rates
(Jetz et al., 2012) without exploring many alternatives (Cooney & Thomas, 2021; Chazot et
al., 2021; Kawahara et al., 2023; Thompson et al., 2024). However, we do agree with the
reviewers that we should aim to set the bar higher and improve those standards by
encouraging sensitivity analyses, when those can be achieved without an excessive time and
computational burden.
For this reason, we indeed explored ways to cross-validate our results using an
alternative approach to BAMM that did not require much more computational time.
Following the framework introduced by Chazot et al., 2021, we performed an entire set of
analyses based on Regional In-situ Radiation (RISR) that aimed to compare diversification
dynamics identified within clades largely restricted to a single bioregion using the R package
diversitree (See Supplementary Information - Section 9.2 RISR analyses). Those analyses
indeed showed that slightly significant diversification dynamics could be identified across
bioregions, which the STRAPP tests conducted on BAMM posterior samples could not detect.
For instance, we showed that the recent Australasian radiations are experiencing currently
higher rates of diversification induced by significant rate increases over time (Fig. 6). This led
to a key point of our conclusion, highlighting that if differences in rates could exist between
bioregions, they tend to mitigate heterogeneity in diversity patterns due to differences in timing
of colonizations (TfAH) rather than being their origin as postulated in the DRH (Table 1; L.
663-673).
Additionally, we also explored GeoSSE and GeoHiSSE approaches (not reported in the
manuscript) as alternative ways to investigate differences in diversification rates across
bioregions. Although these approaches do not allow us to test for differences at different time-
step as our modified STRAPP analyses do, we perceived them as a useful additional layer of
sensitivity testing to add to our study. However, we had to limit tests to the comparison of the
New World vs. Old World (i.e., longitudinal gradient) to limit parameter inflation. We obtained
higher support for a Character InDependent model with two regimes (CID-2) than for a
GeoSSE model. Moreover, the highest support was found for a Character InDependent model
with four regimes (CID-4: the null model against which GeoHiSSE is compared) supporting
our conclusions that no difference of rates across bioregions (here, New World vs. Old World)
are detected (See Table R1 below). However, we did not report those results in the
manuscript because we detected unrealistic parameter estimates in our models with
abnormally high vicariance rates (> 100 events per lineage per My) contrasted with abnormally
low range shift rates (< 0.002 events per lineage per My), while multiple models yielding null
speciation or extinction rates in some regimes. We report here those ill-fitted results to
illustrate to the reviewers that we indeed explored multiple ways to cross-validate our
results with a wealth of complementary approaches and strategies.
Following the reviewers’ suggestions, we now more clearly emphasize the rationale behind
our use of RISR analyses as a means to cross-validate results from BAMM using an
independent approach in the Supplementary Methods (See Section 8.2 BAMM
diversification rates). We believe this clarification highlights our efforts to assess the
robustness of our conclusions in meaningful ways.

We now include a tree displaying BAMM rates and regime shifts identified on the MCC tree in
Supplementary Figure S14. We report the details of the major regime shifts identified from
the Maximum Shift Credibility (MSC) configuration in Supplementary Table S10 and in the
Main text (L. 484-487). We also provide time-calibrated phylogenies displaying the median net
diversification rates as estimated for the two alternative divergence dating hypotheses used
for sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Figure S15).
Additionally, we now provide a figure assessing the MCMC convergence of the BAMM run in
Supplementary Figure S16 as suggested by the reviewers.
We are aware that we have suggested a number of possible additional analyses here, but
these are mostly aimed at strengthening the manuscript and better exploring the limits and
sensitivity of their results. Finally, we would like to congratulate the authors on their work,
which already includes several analyses aimed at better understanding the distribution pattern
of Ponerinae.
We have done our best to include all possible relevant alternative analyses suggested by the
reviewers, within the limit of our time and computational resources. We believe these
additions, combined with the clarification of key methodological choices, have resulted in what
is, to our knowledge, the most thorough and careful examination to date of the limits and
sensitivity of analyses of biogeographic and diversification dynamics for a diverse,
cosmopolitan taxonomic group. We hope that we have respectfully and convincingly
explained why certain proposed alternative methods were ultimately not adopted because: (1)
they would lessen the careful rationale that guided our selection of the most appropriate
approach for each analytic step, (2) they would require computational efforts far beyond
feasible limits, that are not in line with the standards in recent analyses of similar scale and
scope. As stated in the preamble, we sincerely believe that, thanks to the reviewers’ insightful
suggestions, these additions have strengthened our study. We feel that the revised manuscript
now offers an even more robust and transparent blueprint for macroevolutionary
analyses that will hopefully guide many future works.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Dear Editor,
In their manuscript "Timing is everything: Evolution of ponerine ants highlights how dispersal
history shapes modern biodiversity" Doré et al. present the results of a thorough phylogeny-
based analysis of the global historical biogeography of ants in the subfamily Ponerinae.
For their study, the authors first reconstructed phylogenetic relationships and divergence times
among 789 ponerine species and morphospecies using phylogenomic data. Then, they
grafted missing species on the tree based on taxonomic background data, to obtain a "full"
1534-tip tree for ponerine ants. The main analyses are based on the best full dated tree as
well as 1000 posterior "full" trees sampled for estimating the effects of phylogenetic
uncertainty. The authors then estimated ancestral geographic ranges across the fossil-
calibrated trees based on an extensive global database of the distributions of extant ponerine
species. These ancestral reconstructions are combined with phylogeny-based inferences of
diversification rates in past and present lineages, to infer support for three different hypotheses
on the distribution of species diversity observed in the group today. The main conclusion is
that the latitudinal gradient seen in the diversity of extant ponerine ants is mainly the result of
a tendency to remain in the ancestral tropical habitat (tropical niche conservatism), while
asymmetric dispersal and differences in diversification rates have a minor role. The results are
discussed in relation to diversity patterns found in other taxa.
I find the study highly interesting and impressive. The breadth of phylogenetic and statistical
methods covered by the work is breathtaking, but Supplementary figures S1 and S2 do a good
job in explaining how the phylogenetic and biogeographic datasets used in the different
analyses were compiled.
I might have commented on the restriction to net diversification rates and the existence of
megathermal forests in the northern Hemisphere during the early Cenozoic, but both of these
issues are in fact dealt with in the end of the Discussion. These challenges are by no means
restricted to this study, and I find the caveats given in the text sufficient.
I cannot claim to be a specialist in all aspects of the highly diverse statistical analyses, but the
methods used in the parts that I have experience with seem to be up to date, logical and
justified. In some cases, there would be alternative methods available, but these are not
necessarily better than the ones used here. The combined analyses and plots of results from
different statistical methods are highly innovative. To me it seems that such approaches might
be of use also in fields not directly related to biogeography.
Based on the importance of the results and high quality of the data and analyses of the study,
I recommend publication of the manuscript as-is. The supplementary information and scripts
and data files in databases appear to contain all information necessary for replicating the
analyses and results. The manuscript package is so carefully prepared that I struggled to find
even small mistakes or typos from the text, these are listed below.
We thank reviewer #2 for their overall positive review of our manuscript. We particularly
